inputs.source: employee question via SSO authenticated chat
published HR policy documents maintained by HR content team

elements.name: Reply to authenticated requester's chat session
Pinned model and network egress policy configuration

controls.name: Read-only least-privilege credential scoped to policy index
Verified network-layer egress deny outside authenticated chat path
controls.decay_rationale: Independent while enforced at the network layer; only a control removal or introduction of a new output channel would reopen egress.

controls.name: Replies are bound to the authenticated requester's chat session
controls.decay_rationale: The reply destination is fixed by the authenticated chat session rather than model-chosen output.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or auto-fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: Independent client-side restriction that removes common hidden egress channels through rendered content.

controls.name: Two-person review before policy publishing
controls.decay_rationale: Independent editorial workflow limiting tampering of policy content before it enters the index.

controls.name: Model is pinned and changes require a change ticket
controls.decay_rationale: Independent change-management control that prevents silent model upgrades.

controls.name: Missing attributable action audit trail for agent replies
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended audit record would provide attributable provenance for replies; currently absent.

findings.title: Property: no attributable audit trail for agent replies

forecast.watch_signal: Reassess if the agent gains consequential write, execute, spend, delegate, credential, or external egress capabilities; current missing audit trail stays low only because the design reads internal policies and replies only to the authenticated requester.

evidence.observation: Artifacts describe reply routing, network egress denial, model pinning, and credential scope, but do not mention an attributable action log or audit record for agent replies.
The only consequential output described is a chat reply to the authenticated requester, with no other tools, memory, or network egress.

recommendations.action: Add an immutable action log that records agent reply events with agent identity, requester identity, retrieved policy references, and timestamp.

stride_coverage.rationale: The artifacts describe an authenticated employee chat channel but do not state how the agent service identity itself is authenticated to downstream components.
The design exposes only a short bounded Q&A flow with no memory, no spawning, no open-ended runtime, and no spend-bearing or recursive actions.
The case says the chat is SSO authenticated, but it does not provide the identity architecture needed to verify spoofing resistance of employee identities.
The artifacts do not describe requester-side logging or non-repudiation controls for employee chat submissions.
The artifacts identify the HR content team as the source of policies but do not describe identity verification for publishers into the policy workflow.
No publishing audit details are provided for content team actions, so publisher attribution cannot be assessed from the supplied artifacts.
The artifacts do not describe availability protections, quotas, or redundancy for the policy index, so denial-of-service resilience cannot be assessed.
The supplied design facts mention only model pinning and egress policy, with no secrets or sensitive payloads in this store described in the artifacts.
The artifacts do not describe runtime configuration backup, rollout safety, or recovery controls, so service disruption exposure is not assessable.
This input flow is within the authenticated first-party chat boundary as described, and no cross-boundary transport integrity issue is evidenced in the artifacts.
The question flow is described as the employee's authenticated chat session within the same trust domain, so no boundary-crossing disclosure path is evidenced.
The supplied design does not describe this as a boundary-crossing protocol edge or a bottlenecked external channel requiring separate flow-level DoS analysis.
Policy retrieval is described as internal read-only access to the published index, not a boundary-crossing transport where in-transit tampering is evidenced.
The policy retrieval flow remains inside the trust domain and reads only internal published policies, so no cross-boundary disclosure issue is evidenced.
This is not described as a boundary-crossing flow, and the supplied artifacts give no separate transport-level DoS condition to assess.
The reply flow is constrained to the authenticated requester's chat session inside the described environment, with no separate boundary-crossing transport risk evidenced.
The reply path is limited to the authenticated requester and is not described as crossing a trust boundary, so a flow-level cross-boundary disclosure entry does not apply.
The design gives no evidence of a separate boundary-crossing reply transport or queue whose capacity would require independent DoS treatment.

rating.rationale: Manual validation applied from the checklist because scripts could not be run. Reviewed prompt, tool manifest, and runtime notes. No untrusted source reaches a sensitive sink today: the employee question is a trusted authenticated input, the only tool is read-only search over internal published policies, replies are bound to the authenticated requester's session, the client removes common hidden egress channels, and verified network-layer egress denial severs outbound exfiltration paths. The only present finding is a low property finding for missing attributable reply audit records. Forecast stays low for the assessed design; the most important change trigger to watch is any new tool or data-scope expansion, which would require reassessment before this low rating can be relied on.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior except where the artifacts explicitly state verification such as the reported pen test for network egress denial.

No source code, infrastructure-as-code, protocol configuration, or logging configuration was provided, so identity, audit, and availability properties could only be assessed from documentation-level statements.
Because no runtime telemetry or test evidence beyond the stated pen test was supplied, confidence is lower for properties that depend on operational implementation rather than the documented design.
